full.text: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace proposed that species change over time by natural selection.

items: Organisms produce more offspring than can survive
Individuals in a population show *variation*, much of it inherited
There is competition for limited resources (struggle for existence)
Individuals with favourable variations survive and reproduce more (survival of the fittest)
Favourable alleles become more common over generations

full.text: The process by which organisms better adapted to their environment survive and reproduce more, so their inherited traits become more common.
Antibiotic resistance: bacteria with a resistance mutation survive treatment and multiply, so the resistant form spreads.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Selection acts on the phenotype of individuals, but it is the population that evolves. Do not write that an individual adapts by choice.
Organisms are grouped into a hierarchy of taxa: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Linnaeus introduced the two-part scientific name: genus name (capital letter) and specific epithet (small letter), written in italics or underlined when handwritten.
Scientific names are universal, so scientists everywhere know which organism is meant.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: When you write a binomial name by hand, underline the genus and species separately.

items: Hierarchy: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Species: interbreed to give fertile offspring
Binomial name: Genus species, italics or underlined

full.text: Fungi are eukaryotic, heterotrophic organisms that absorb food after external digestion.

items: Body made of thread-like *hyphae* forming a *mycelium* (except yeasts, which are unicellular)
Store food as glycogen and lipids
Reproduce by spores, asexually and sexually

full.text: An organism that feeds on dead organic matter by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products.
Fungi are decomposers that recycle nutrients. Yeast is used in baking and brewing, and Penicillium gives penicillin. Some fungi cause diseases of crops and humans.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Mention chitin and absorptive nutrition when comparing fungi with plants.

items: Hyphae form mycelium; yeast is unicellular

written.stem: Outline Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection.
written.model_answer: Organisms overproduce offspring; individuals show inherited variation; there is a struggle for existence; those with favourable variations survive and reproduce; so favourable traits become more common over generations.

points.text: Favourable traits survive, reproduce and increase

written.stem: Explain the rules of binomial nomenclature with an example.
written.model_answer: Each organism has two names: genus (capital first letter) and species (small letter), written in italics or underlined separately when handwritten, for example Homo sapiens.

points.text: Genus starts with a capital letter
Italics or underlined, with an example

written.stem: List four features that distinguish fungi from plants.
written.model_answer: Fungi have cell walls of chitin, not cellulose; they are heterotrophic with no chlorophyll; they absorb food after external digestion; they store glycogen, not starch; their body is made of hyphae.

written.stem: Distinguish between homologous and analogous structures, giving one example of each.
written.model_answer: Homologous structures have the same origin but may have different functions, for example the forelimbs of humans, whales and bats. Analogous structures have the same function but different origins, for example the wings of birds and insects.

points.text: Example of analogous (wings of bird and insect)

written.stem: Explain how natural selection can lead to the formation of a new species.
written.model_answer: A population becomes separated, for example by a geographical barrier. Each group shows variation and faces different selection pressures, so different alleles are favoured. Mutations and genetic drift add differences. Over many generations the groups become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so a new species has formed (allopatric speciation).

points.text: Reproductive isolation: cannot interbreed fertile offspring

written.stem: Describe the main features of the three domains of life.
written.model_answer: Bacteria are prokaryotes with peptidoglycan walls and 70S ribosomes. Archaea are prokaryotes without peptidoglycan, often in extreme habitats, with membrane lipids different from bacteria. Eukarya have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, 80S ribosomes, and include protists, fungi, plants and animals.

points.text: Archaea: prokaryotic, no peptidoglycan, extreme habitats

ask.question: What is natural selection?
ask.answer: Natural selection is the process by which individuals with inherited variations that suit their environment survive and reproduce more, so those variations become more common in the population over generations.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 3.3: Natural selection and Darwinian theory

ask.question: What is binomial nomenclature?
ask.answer: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part scientific name: the genus (with a capital letter) and the species (in small letters), written in italics, for example Homo sapiens. It was introduced by Linnaeus.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 3.5: Classification and binomial nomenclature

ask.question: What are the features of fungi?
ask.answer: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs with cell walls of chitin. Most are made of hyphae forming a mycelium, they digest food outside the body and absorb it, store glycogen and reproduce by spores.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 3.8: Kingdom Fungi

ask.question: What are the three domains of life?
ask.answer: The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes; Archaea lack peptidoglycan in their cell walls. Eukarya have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 3.6: Three domains of life

ask.question: How do new species form?
ask.answer: New species form when populations become reproductively isolated, for example by a geographical barrier. Different selection pressures and mutations change each population until they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

uploads.title: Evolution by natural selection
uploads.summary: These notes explain Darwin and Wallace's theory of natural selection, the evidence for evolution and how new species can form.
key_points: Variation is inherited and selection acts on it
Fossils, homologous structures and molecular data are evidence
Isolation can lead to new species
Antibiotic resistance is a modern example
